lessonTitle: CT, MRI and Ultrasound of the Musculoskeletal System

blocks.text: Two patients arrive on the same afternoon. One has fallen from a ladder onto his heel and the plain film suggests a crushed calcaneus; the other twisted her knee playing netball and cannot straighten it. Both need more than a plain film, yet they need different scans, because one problem is in bone and the other in ligament and cartilage.

blocks.markdown: Plain radiographs show bone well but cannot show ligaments, tendons, menisci or cartilage directly. Three further techniques fill the gap. **Computed tomography (CT)** builds cross-sectional images from many X-ray projections. **Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)** uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves, and creates images from the behaviour of hydrogen nuclei in tissue water and fat. **Ultrasound** uses high-frequency sound waves that are reflected at tissue boundaries. Each technique has its own strengths, limits and safety issues.

rows: CT
X-rays and a rotating detector; images are slices that can be reformatted in 3D
Excellent detail of cortical bone and complex fractures (for example intra-articular fractures, spine, pelvis, calcaneus); fast
Ionising radiation; poorer soft tissue contrast than MRI
MRI
Magnetic field and radio waves; signals from hydrogen in water and fat
Best soft tissue contrast: ligaments, tendons, menisci, cartilage, muscle, bone marrow; detects occult fractures and bone marrow oedema; no ionising radiation
Expensive, long scan times; contraindications (some pacemakers and ferromagnetic implants); claustrophobia; less detail of cortical bone than CT
Ultrasound
Sound waves reflected by tissue interfaces
Real-time and dynamic imaging of superficial tendons, muscles, joint effusions; no ionising radiation; portable and cheap; guides injections and aspirations
Cannot penetrate bone or air; operator-dependent; limited view of deep structures and the inside of joints
blocks.caption: Comparison of CT, MRI and ultrasound for the musculoskeletal system.

blocks.title: Choose the modality for the question being asked
blocks.text: Bone detail and complex fractures: CT. Ligament, meniscus, cartilage, marrow or occult fracture: MRI. Superficial tendon, muscle or effusion, especially when dynamic assessment, bedside examination or guided injection is helpful: ultrasound. Radiation exposure is a factor for CT but not for MRI or ultrasound.

blocks.markdown: **Reading a limb cross-section.** CT and MRI limb images are usually **axial** (transverse) slices. By convention they are displayed as if the viewer is looking from the patient's feet upward, so the **patient's right side is on the left of the image**; the anterior surface is at the top. Identify the bone first, then the compartments around it. In a **mid-thigh** slice, the femur lies centrally. The **anterior compartment** (quadriceps femoris and sartorius) lies in front, the **medial compartment** (adductors and gracilis) on the inner side, and the **posterior compartment** (hamstrings) behind, with the sciatic nerve between the hamstrings and the adductor magnus. The femoral vessels run in the anteromedial thigh, in the subsartorial region. In the **mid-arm**, the humerus is central, with biceps brachii and brachialis in front and triceps behind. In the **mid-leg**, the tibia is anteromedial and the fibula lateral, joined by the interosseous membrane, with the four compartments around them.

blocks.title: Orienting a CT slice
blocks.prompt: A mid-thigh axial image is displayed with the femur in the centre. A large muscle group lies behind it, with a smaller group on the inner side. Which muscles are they, and how do you know which side of the patient is which?

steps.text: On axial images the front is at the top, so the large group behind the femur is the posterior compartment, the hamstrings.
The group on the inner (medial) side is the adductor compartment, which includes adductor longus, brevis, magnus and gracilis.
Images are viewed from the feet upwards, so the patient's right is on the left of the image: use the side marker to confirm.

blocks.answer: The hamstrings (posterior) and adductors (medial); the patient's right appears on the left of the image.

blocks.markdown: **Joint structures on MRI.** In a knee MRI, the **menisci** appear as dark (low-signal) triangular wedges at the joint margins on sagittal images. The **anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments** are seen as dark bands crossing the joint in the intercondylar notch. **Articular cartilage** is a thin layer of intermediate signal covering the bone ends, and **bone marrow oedema** (from a recent injury) shows as an area of bright signal on fluid-sensitive images. **Joint effusion** appears bright on the same sequences. On ultrasound, a healthy tendon shows a regular, fibrillar echo pattern, while a tear appears as a gap or a disrupted, hypoechoic (dark) area; the tendon can be examined during movement.

rows: Suspected ACL tear or meniscal tear
MRI
Shows intra-articular ligaments, menisci and cartilage without radiation
Suspected rotator cuff tear
Ultrasound or MRI
Ultrasound shows the superficial tendon dynamically; MRI shows the whole joint
Suspected Achilles tendon rupture or tendinopathy
Ultrasound (or MRI)
Superficial tendon, can be examined at the bedside during movement
Complex fracture of the calcaneus or tibial plateau
CT
Best definition of cortical bone and fragment position; 3D planning
Suspected scaphoid fracture with a normal radiograph
MRI (or CT)
Detects occult fractures and marrow oedema
blocks.caption: Selecting a modality for specific questions.

blocks.title: Selecting the scan
blocks.prompt: A 28-year-old footballer twists his knee, hears a pop and develops a swollen knee that gives way. A radiograph shows no fracture. Which imaging modality would best show a ligament injury, and why not CT?

steps.text: The suspected injury is of the ACL and possibly the meniscus, which are soft tissues inside the joint.
MRI gives the best contrast between ligament, cartilage, meniscus and fluid and uses no ionising radiation.
CT is best for bone, with poorer soft tissue contrast and ionising radiation, so it is not the best choice.

blocks.answer: MRI, because it best shows intra-articular ligaments and menisci without radiation.

items: CT: best for cortical bone and complex fractures; uses ionising radiation.
MRI: best soft tissue contrast (ligament, meniscus, cartilage, marrow); no ionising radiation; avoid with some implants.
Ultrasound: real-time, dynamic assessment of superficial tendons and muscles; portable; no ionising radiation.
Axial images are viewed from the feet; the patient's right is on the left of the image.

blocks.title: Safety and practical limits
blocks.text: MRI must not be used until a patient has been screened for pacemakers, certain implants, and metal fragments in the eye or body. CT involves a higher radiation dose than plain radiography, so the benefit must justify the exposure, especially in children and pregnancy. Ultrasound cannot see through bone or air, so it cannot show the inside of a joint behind bone.

points: CT shows cortical bone and complex fractures best, MRI shows soft tissues (ligament, meniscus, cartilage, marrow) best, and ultrasound shows superficial tendons and muscles in real time.
Axial limb images are viewed from the feet, so the patient's right is on the left of the image; identify the bone first and then the muscle compartments around it.
Choose the modality by the clinical question: ACL or meniscal injury suggests MRI, superficial tendon injury suggests ultrasound or MRI, and a complex fracture suggests CT.

questions.stem: Which imaging modality gives the best detail of cortical bone and complex fractures?

distractorRationale.c: MRI is better for soft tissues and marrow, with less detail of cortical bone.

questions.explanation: CT is based on X-ray attenuation and is very good at showing cortical bone and fragment position, with 3D reformatting. This makes it the first choice for complex intra-articular fractures.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old footballer has a swollen knee that gives way after a twisting injury. The radiograph is normal. Which investigation best shows a suspected ACL or meniscal tear?

distractorRationale.b: CT shows bone well but soft tissue contrast is poor.
distractorRationale.c: Ultrasound cannot visualise the deep intra-articular structures behind bone.
distractorRationale.d: Plain radiographs do not show ligaments or menisci.

questions.explanation: MRI has the best soft tissue contrast and shows the cruciate ligaments, menisci, cartilage and marrow oedema. It uses no ionising radiation.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of ultrasound for imaging the musculoskeletal system?

options.text: Real-time, dynamic imaging with no ionising radiation

questions.correctOptionText: Real-time, dynamic imaging with no ionising radiation

distractorRationale.b: Sound does not penetrate bone well.

questions.explanation: Ultrasound can be performed at the bedside, can show a tendon moving, and uses no ionising radiation. Its limits are poor penetration of bone and dependence on the operator.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a contraindication to MRI?

options.text: A pacemaker or ferromagnetic implant that is not MRI-compatible

questions.correctOptionText: A pacemaker or ferromagnetic implant that is not MRI-compatible

distractorRationale.b: Pregnancy is a concern for ionising radiation rather than being an absolute contraindication to MRI.
distractorRationale.c: A healed fracture does not prevent MRI.
distractorRationale.d: An effusion is a common indication for MRI.

questions.explanation: The strong magnetic field can move or heat ferromagnetic implants and can interfere with some pacemakers. Patients must be screened before an MRI scan.

questions.stem: How are axial CT or MRI slices of a limb conventionally displayed?

options.text: As if viewed from the patient's feet, with the patient's right on the left of the image
As if viewed from the patient's head, with the patient's right on the right of the image
With the posterior surface at the top and the patient's left on the left

questions.correctOptionText: As if viewed from the patient's feet, with the patient's right on the left of the image

distractorRationale.b: Axial images are viewed from below, not from above.
distractorRationale.c: The anterior surface is conventionally at the top.

questions.explanation: Axial images are displayed as if you stand at the patient's feet looking up, so the patient's right is on the left of the image and the anterior surface is at the top. Use side markers to confirm.

questions.stem: On an axial mid-thigh image with the femur in the centre, which muscle group lies directly behind the femur?

distractorRationale.b: Quadriceps lies in front of the femur.
distractorRationale.c: The adductors and gracilis lie on the medial side.
distractorRationale.d: Tibialis anterior is in the leg, not the thigh.

questions.explanation: The posterior compartment of the thigh contains the hamstrings, lying behind the femur on an axial image where the front is at the top. The sciatic nerve lies in this compartment.

questions.stem: A runner has pain at the back of the heel and the calf squeeze test is abnormal, suggesting an Achilles tendon rupture. Which first-line modality allows a bedside dynamic assessment of the tendon?

distractorRationale.b: CT has poor soft tissue contrast and uses radiation.
distractorRationale.c: A bone scan is not used for tendon assessment and is not covered in this lesson.
distractorRationale.d: A plain radiograph cannot show a tendon tear directly.

questions.explanation: The Achilles tendon is superficial, so ultrasound shows its fibres clearly and can examine it during movement. MRI is also suitable when more detail is needed.

questions.stem: True or false: MRI uses ionising radiation to produce its images.

distractorRationale.a: MRI uses a magnetic field and radio waves, which are non-ionising.

questions.explanation: MRI uses a strong magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses, not ionising radiation. CT uses X-rays and so involves ionising radiation.

questions.stem: Compare CT, MRI and ultrasound in imaging bone and soft tissue, giving one strength and one limitation of each.
markingGuide: CT: excellent cortical bone and complex fractures; uses ionising radiation and has poorer soft tissue contrast.
MRI: best soft tissue contrast (ligaments, tendons, menisci, cartilage, marrow); no ionising radiation; expensive, long scans, implant contraindications.
Ultrasound: real-time dynamic imaging of superficial tendons and muscle, portable, no ionising radiation; cannot penetrate bone and is operator-dependent.
questions.explanation: Each modality is based on a different physical principle, so each shows different tissues best. Choosing a modality is about matching the strength to the clinical question.

questions.stem: A patient is suspected of having an anterior cruciate ligament tear, and another of having a supraspinatus tendon tear. Select an appropriate imaging modality for each and justify your choice.
markingGuide: ACL: MRI, because it shows intra-articular ligaments, menisci and cartilage with high soft tissue contrast and no ionising radiation.
Ultrasound is limited here because it cannot visualise deep intra-articular structures through bone; CT has poor soft tissue contrast.
Supraspinatus: ultrasound (superficial tendon, dynamic, portable) or MRI (whole joint).
Plain radiograph is used first to exclude fracture but cannot show the ligament or tendon.
questions.explanation: The choice depends on the depth and type of structure: deep intra-articular ligaments need MRI, whereas a superficial tendon can be examined with ultrasound. In both cases a plain film may be taken first to exclude fracture.
